subject: Human Performance
syllabus_version: CAP 1298 (published 2015-05), Subject 2 Human Performance - Basic Aviation Physiology (currency not re-verified against a more recent UK CAA publication this session; see source notes)
question_text: Which of the following is a classic early symptom of hypoxia that makes it particularly dangerous for pilots?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sharp, localised chest pain

choices.label: B
choices.text: A false sense of well-being (euphoria) and impaired judgement

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immediate and total loss of consciousness

choices.label: D
choices.text: Uncontrollable shivering

explanation: An early and particularly hazardous symptom of hypoxia is euphoria — an unwarranted sense of well-being that impairs judgement, often before the pilot notices any other physical symptom, making self-recognition difficult.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Chest pain is not a characteristic early hypoxia symptom.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Hypoxia develops progressively; sudden total loss of consciousness is a late-stage outcome, not an early symptom.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Shivering is associated with cold exposure/hypothermia, not hypoxia.

subject: Human Performance
syllabus_version: CAP 1298 (published 2015-05), Subject 2 Human Performance - Basic Aviation Physiology
learning_objective: Hyperventilation - state the underlying physiological cause.
question_text: Hyperventilation in flight is most directly caused by

choices.label: A
choices.text: breathing in excess of the body's metabolic needs, lowering blood carbon dioxide levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: breathing too slowly, causing carbon dioxide to build up in the blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: a sudden drop in cabin oxygen partial pressure

choices.label: D
choices.text: an excess of carbon monoxide in the bloodstream

explanation: Hyperventilation is over-breathing relative to the body's metabolic needs, which washes out carbon dioxide from the blood faster than it is produced, disturbing the blood's acid-base balance and producing symptoms such as dizziness, tingling, and muscle spasms.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Under-breathing would raise, not lower, blood CO2, and describes a different (hypoventilation) condition, not hyperventilation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A drop in oxygen partial pressure describes hypoxia's cause, which is a distinct condition from hyperventilation, though the two can have overlapping symptoms and occur together.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Carbon monoxide poisoning is a separate toxic hazard, not the mechanism of hyperventilation.

subject: Human Performance
syllabus_version: CAP 1298 (published 2015-05), Subject 2 Human Performance - Basic Aviation Physiology
learning_objective: Spatial disorientation - describe the somatogravic illusion.
question_text: During a rapid acceleration on takeoff in poor visual conditions, a pilot may experience the illusion that the aircraft is

choices.label: A
choices.text: yawing to the left

choices.label: B
choices.text: pitching nose-up, even though it is flying level

choices.label: C
choices.text: descending, even though it is climbing

choices.label: D
choices.text: rolling to the right

explanation: This is the somatogravic illusion: forward acceleration stimulates the inner ear's otolith organs in a way that is indistinguishable from a nose-up pitch, causing the pilot to feel the aircraft is pitching up even when it is flying level or actually pitching down slightly — a hazard that can prompt an inappropriate nose-down correction.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The somatogravic illusion is a pitch (fore-aft) illusion, not a yaw sensation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The illusion associated with forward acceleration is a false sense of climbing/pitching up, not descending.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The somatogravic illusion is not a roll sensation; it results from linear acceleration, not banking.

subject: Human Performance
syllabus_version: CAP 1298 (published 2015-05), Subject 2 Human Performance - Basic Aviation Physiology
learning_objective: Sleep and fatigue - describe the effect of fatigue on pilot performance.
question_text: Which of the following is most characteristic of the effect of fatigue on a pilot's performance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Improved reaction time but reduced fine motor control

choices.label: B
choices.text: Narrowed attention, slower decision-making, and reduced ability to detect errors

choices.label: C
choices.text: No measurable effect until the pilot is completely asleep

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased tolerance for risk-taking only, with no other cognitive effect

explanation: Fatigue progressively narrows attention, slows decision-making, degrades short-term memory, and reduces a pilot's ability to notice and correct their own errors — effects that can be present well before a pilot feels overtly sleepy.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Fatigue degrades, rather than improves, reaction time.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Fatigue's effects on cognition and performance are measurable well before the point of falling asleep.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Fatigue affects multiple cognitive functions (attention, memory, decision-making), not merely risk tolerance.

subject: Human Performance
syllabus_version: CAP 1298 (published 2015-05), Subject 2 Human Performance - Basic Aviation Psychology
learning_objective: Hazardous attitudes - identify the 'invulnerability' attitude and its antidote.
question_text: A pilot who thinks, "Accidents happen to other people, not to me," is displaying which hazardous attitude, and what is the recommended antidote thought?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-authority; antidote: 'Follow the rules, they are usually right.'

choices.label: B
choices.text: Invulnerability; antidote: 'It could happen to me.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: Macho; antidote: 'Taking chances is foolish.'

choices.label: D
choices.text: Resignation; antidote: 'I'm not helpless, I can make a difference.'

explanation: The belief that accidents happen only to others is the classic description of the invulnerability hazardous attitude; its recommended antidote thought is 'It could happen to me,' encouraging realistic personal risk assessment.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Anti-authority is characterized by resentment of rules ('don't tell me'), not a belief in personal immunity to accidents.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Macho is characterized by a need to prove oneself ('I can do it'), a different attitude from believing accidents only happen to others.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Resignation is characterized by a feeling of helplessness ('what's the use'), the opposite orientation from believing oneself immune to harm.

subject: Human Performance
syllabus_version: CAP 1298 (published 2015-05), Subject 2 Human Performance - Principles of Threat and Error Management
learning_objective: Threat and Error Management - define an 'undesired aircraft state.'
question_text: In Threat and Error Management (TEM), an 'undesired aircraft state' is best described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: any deviation from what ATC has cleared, regardless of safety significance

choices.label: B
choices.text: a position, configuration, or speed deviation that reduces the safety margin, resulting from an ineffectively managed threat or error

choices.label: C
choices.text: any mechanical malfunction of the aircraft

choices.label: D
choices.text: a deliberate manoeuvre briefed in advance

explanation: An undesired aircraft state is a flight-crew-induced position, configuration, or speed deviation that reduces safety margins, typically arising when a threat or error was not effectively detected and managed — it is a key concept linking threats and errors to actual safety outcomes in the TEM model.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Not every ATC deviation is safety-significant; TEM specifically concerns states that reduce safety margins.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A mechanical malfunction is itself a potential threat, not the definition of an undesired aircraft state (though it could lead to one if mismanaged).
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A briefed, deliberate manoeuvre is not 'undesired' by definition.

subject: Human Performance
syllabus_version: CAP 1298 (published 2015-05), Subject 2 Human Performance - Principles of Threat and Error Management
learning_objective: Decision making - describe the role of situational awareness.
question_text: A pilot who has lost situational awareness is most accurately described as one who

choices.label: A
choices.text: no longer has an accurate understanding of what is happening around the aircraft and where that situation may be heading

choices.label: B
choices.text: has become too focused on a single instrument to the exclusion of all others

choices.label: C
choices.text: has stopped communicating with air traffic control

choices.label: D
choices.text: has exceeded the aircraft's structural limitations

explanation: Situational awareness is the pilot's accurate perception and understanding of the current flight situation and how it is likely to develop; losing it means the pilot's mental picture no longer matches reality, which can lead to poor decisions even when individual actions seem locally reasonable.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Excessive fixation on one instrument (a form of attentional tunnelling) is one possible CAUSE of lost situational awareness, but is not itself the definition of the concept.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Loss of radio communication is a separate operational issue, not the definition of lost situational awareness.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Exceeding structural limits is a possible consequence of poor decision-making, not the definition of situational awareness.

subject: Human Performance
syllabus_version: CAP 1298 (published 2015-05), Subject 2 Human Performance - Basic Aviation Physiology
learning_objective: Vision and visual illusions - explain dark adaptation and its relevance to night flying.
question_text: A pilot preparing for a night flight should be aware that full dark adaptation of the eyes typically takes approximately

choices.label: A
choices.text: 30 seconds

choices.label: B
choices.text: 5 minutes

choices.label: C
choices.text: 30 minutes

choices.label: D
choices.text: 3 hours

explanation: Full dark adaptation, during which the eyes' rod cells become maximally sensitive to low light, takes approximately 30 minutes; exposure to bright light (including cockpit lighting or a phone screen) can quickly undo this adaptation.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 30 seconds is far too short for full dark adaptation; some adaptation begins quickly but full sensitivity takes much longer.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 5 minutes achieves only partial adaptation, not the full adaptation typically cited.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 3 hours substantially overstates the time required; adaptation is essentially complete well before this.

subject: Human Performance
syllabus_version: CAP 1298 (published 2015-05), Subject 2 Human Performance - Basic Aviation Physiology
learning_objective: Toxic hazards - identify symptoms of carbon monoxide exposure in a piston-engine aircraft.
question_text: A pilot of a piston-engine aeroplane with a heater fed by exhaust-manifold air begins to feel a dull headache and drowsiness in cruise flight with the cabin heat on. This most likely indicates

choices.label: A
choices.text: hyperventilation from over-breathing

choices.label: B
choices.text: possible carbon monoxide exposure from a leaking exhaust/heater system

choices.label: C
choices.text: a normal reaction to reduced cabin humidity

choices.label: D
choices.text: the onset of decompression sickness

explanation: Headache, drowsiness, and dizziness during flight with cabin heat drawn from around the exhaust system are classic early signs of carbon monoxide exposure from a leak in the exhaust/heat-exchanger system; the pilot should shut off cabin heat, ventilate with fresh air, and land as soon as practicable.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Hyperventilation is typically linked to over-breathing/anxiety, not specifically to cabin heat use, and does not explain the specific headache/drowsiness combination in this context as well as CO exposure does.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Reduced humidity causes dryness/irritation, not headache and drowsiness of this nature.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Decompression sickness is associated with rapid pressure changes and is not a typical light-aircraft piston-cruise scenario.

subject: Human Performance
syllabus_version: CAP 1298 (published 2015-05), Subject 2 Human Performance - Basic Aviation Psychology
learning_objective: Stress and stress management - describe the effect of increasing stress on performance.
question_text: According to the general relationship between arousal/stress and performance taught in human-factors training, a pilot's performance is typically best when arousal is

choices.label: A
choices.text: as low as possible, since any stress degrades performance

choices.label: B
choices.text: at a moderate level; performance falls off at both very low and very high arousal

choices.label: C
choices.text: as high as possible, since more stress always sharpens focus

choices.label: D
choices.text: irrelevant, since performance depends only on skill level, not arousal

explanation: The classic arousal-performance relationship (often shown as an inverted-U curve) indicates that performance is poor at very low arousal (boredom, complacency) and also poor at very high arousal/stress (narrowed attention, panic), with a moderate level of arousal producing the best performance.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Some arousal is beneficial for alertness; the relationship is not simply 'less is always better.'
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Excessive stress degrades performance through tunnel vision and impaired decision-making; more stress is not always better.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Arousal/stress level measurably affects performance independent of underlying skill, per the standard model taught in this subject.
